lesson.title: D→T Discrimination Drills
lesson.subtitle: The five-shift gauntlet: which rule, which direction, at full speed

hook.title: The Gauntlet
hook.content: You now own all five great shifts — P→F, TH→D, T→S, K→CH, D→T — plus the double-shift rule. Today is the gauntlet: mixed words, both directions, no labels. German Tag meets English day through TWO shifts at once (d → t and y → g). German Tisch meets English dish through a Latin detour. The words are all old friends; the game is naming the machinery instantly, the way a musician names a chord without counting the notes.

footnotes.title: Tag's Double Life
footnotes.content: Tag hides two shifts: the d of day hardened to t, and the ancient g that English wore down to y (day, way, say) still growls at the end of Tag. English vocalized the g; German kept it audible.

pattern.title: Name That Shift
pattern.content: Mixed deck, rapid fire: day → Tag (D→T + Y→G), door → Tür (D→T), drink → trinken (D→T), garden/yard → Garten (medial D→T), cold → kalt (final D→T), good → gut (final D→T), word → Wort (final D→T), dream → Traum (D→T), dish/board → Tisch (the Latin discus detour: English dish kept d, German hardened to t). Now reverse it: every German t-word you meet, test d first — Tod/dead, tief/deep, Tochter/daughter, Traum/dream, trinken/drink.
pattern.linguist_note: Direction matters: German d usually answers to English th (TH→D), while English d answers to German t (D→T). When both languages show the same consonant (Hand, Arm, Wasser-era words aside), the word simply sat in a safe seat.

exercises.prompt: The gauntlet, round one — match at speed (the last one runs a different shift — spot it):
exercises.explanation: Final, initial, and medial d all hardened to t — and Tisch took the Latin discus detour.

exercises.prompt: English 'day' and German 'Tag' — how many shifts separate them?
options: Three: D → T, T → S, K → CH
Two: D → T and Y → G
exercises.target_answer: Two: D → T and Y → G
exercises.explanation: The d hardened to t, and the ancient g that English vocalized to y still sounds at the end of Tag.

exercises.prompt: Select EVERY honest English rendering of this German sentence (watch out for tense traps):
renderings: I am drinking cold water today
traps: I will drink cold water today
exercises.meaning: I drink / am drinking cold water today
exercises.explanation: German present tense (ich trinke) covers both English simple present ('I drink') and progressive ('I am drinking'). [Ref: Swap ch back to k: the k → CH shelf — riechen is 'reek' (to smell)]

exercises.prompt: What four-letter English noun meaning 'a unit of language' is the D→T twin of 'Wort'?
exercises.explanation: word → Wort: the final d hardened to t. English kept the soft d; German closed it.

vocab_hints.note: der Traum — masculine, like English 'the dream'

exercises.explanation: Two t-words, two stories: Traum is a D→T word, tief a D→T + P→F double — both answering to English d and p.

summary.outcome: Run all five shifts in both directions at speed, including double shifts.
summary.takeaway: German t? Test English d. German d? Test English th. Every letter is a receipt of one specific law.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the Latin Bridge — how French courtly culture handed you 500 German verbs ending in -ieren.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from D→T Discrimination Drills (The dream is deep):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Traum ist tief" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of D→T Discrimination Drills without relying on short-term echo.

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

tür.etymology_derivation: d → t with vowel mutation to ü.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

garten.context_translation: The children play in the garden.

wort.etymology_derivation: Final d → t. Plural: Wörter / Worte.

tisch.context_phrase: Der Teller steht auf dem Tisch.
tisch.context_translation: The plate stands on the table.
tisch.etymology_derivation: Latin discus → Old English disc (dish/desk) → Old High German tisc (tisch, with d → t).

tief.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and p → f.

tochter.context_phrase: Meine Tochter lernt in der Schule.
tochter.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and gh → ch.

knochen.context_phrase: Der Hund kaut an einem Knochen.
knochen.context_translation: The dog is chewing on a bone.
knochen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *knokō 'bone, joint' — cognate with English knuckle; German k shifted to ch. [wiktionary]

riechen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German riohhan, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. English reek is a listed cognate, keeping the k where German shifted to ch. [wiktionary]

koch.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kok — a true k → ch shift word (cook ↔ Koch). [wiktionary]

kauen.context_phrase: Kau dein Essen langsam und gut.
kauen.context_translation: Chew your food slowly and well.
kauen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *keuwan, PIE *ǵyewh₁-; the page lists English chew as cognate — English palatalized the old k to ch, German kept it as k. [wiktionary]

kälte.context_phrase: Ich hasse die Kälte im Winter.
kälte.context_translation: I hate the cold in winter.
kälte.etymology_derivation: Kalt (cold) plus -e; kalt is the twin of English cold with English d become German t (the d-to-t shift); the page says perhaps comparable to English cold. [wiktionary]

mittag.context_phrase: Wir essen um zwölf Uhr zu Mittag.
mittag.context_translation: We eat lunch at twelve o'clock.
mittag.etymology_derivation: Mitt(e) + Tag, literally middle-day — the exact structural twin of English midday; Tag is the twin of day (d → t). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
